reference.source: Standard paediatric gastroenterology and allergy reference texts
clinicalPearls: A non-IgE-mediated food allergy presenting in early infancy with blood-streaked, sometimes mucousy, stools in an otherwise well, thriving baby
It is most commonly caused by cow's milk protein, and many affected infants are breast-fed and react to protein passed through maternal milk
The infant is characteristically well, feeding normally and gaining weight, and is not systemically unwell despite the visible blood
Bleeding is usually low-volume and significant anaemia is uncommon
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by resolution of bleeding after removing the culprit protein and recurrence on reintroduction
In breast-fed infants, maternal exclusion of cow's milk and sometimes soy is first-line, while formula-fed infants are switched to an extensively hydrolysed formula
Allergy tests such as skin-prick and specific IgE are usually negative because the process is non-IgE-mediated
The prognosis is excellent, with most infants tolerating the protein and the condition resolving within the first year or two of life
reference.pathophysiology: Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis is a non-IgE-mediated, eosinophil-predominant immune response to dietary food proteins, most often cow's milk protein reaching the infant directly or through breast milk. The reaction is localised to the distal colon and rectum, where mucosal inflammation causes friability and small-vessel bleeding, producing blood-streaked stools. The condition is benign and self-limiting and is not associated with systemic illness or, in most cases, significant blood loss.
additionalDifferentials: Infective colitis from organisms such as Salmonella or Campylobacter
Necrotising enterocolitis, especially in the preterm or unwell neonate
Swallowed maternal blood in the breast-fed newborn
Intussusception or another surgical cause of rectal bleeding
Coagulopathy or vitamin K deficiency bleeding
Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome or other food allergy
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment confirming a well, thriving infant, which is the key discriminator
Trial of dietary protein elimination with documented resolution of bleeding
Full blood count to check for anaemia or eosinophilia when bleeding is notable
Stool culture and microscopy to exclude infective causes
Sigmoidoscopy with biopsy only in atypical or non-resolving cases, which shows eosinophilic infiltration
Planned reintroduction or rechallenge to confirm the diagnosis where appropriate
redFlags: A systemically unwell or febrile infant
Significant or large-volume rectal bleeding, or anaemia
Poor weight gain or faltering growth
Abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, or other signs of obstruction
Bleeding that does not resolve despite appropriate dietary elimination
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent: this is a benign, self-limiting condition, and most infants outgrow it and tolerate the protein by around one to two years of age with no lasting sequelae.
pitfalls: Over-investigating a well, thriving infant with typical features
Attributing all infant rectal bleeding to allergy and missing a fissure, infection, or surgical cause
Stopping breast-feeding unnecessarily instead of adjusting the maternal diet
Not allowing enough time on elimination before judging the response
Failing to plan a supervised reintroduction to confirm resolution and tolerance
references: International guidance on cow's milk protein allergy
Standard paediatric gastroenterology and allergy reference texts
